reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented five-year comparison. Option A is a subscription at $40,000 a year with $30,000 of implementation, $10,000 of training, 0.1 of an administrator's time ($15,000 a year at a fully loaded $150,000) and $10,000 to retire it. Option B is free to license but needs $80,000 of implementation, $10,000 of training, $12,000 a year of hosting, 0.4 of an administrator ($60,000 a year) and $20,000 to retire. Discounting and risk are left out.

Derivation: Option A costs 30,000 + 10,000 + 5 × (40,000 + 15,000) + 10,000 = $325,000. Option B costs 80,000 + 10,000 + 5 × (12,000 + 60,000) + 20,000 = $470,000. Judged by license price alone, B looks $200,000 cheaper; counted over its life, it costs $145,000 more.

Independent check by year: A is $95,000 in year 1 (30,000 + 10,000 + 55,000) and $55,000 in each of years 2 to 5, which with $10,000 of retirement gives 95,000 + 220,000 + 10,000 = $325,000. B is $162,000 in year 1 and $72,000 a year after that: 162,000 + 288,000 + 20,000 = $470,000. Both routes agree.

Misconception to reject: 'the option with the lowest purchase price is the cheapest.' Labor, hosting, support and retirement continue for the whole life of a system, and for information technology they are often larger than the purchase.

Change one factor: if Option B needed only 0.2 of an administrator ($30,000 a year), it would cost 90,000 + 5 × 42,000 + 20,000 = $320,000, slightly less than A. The decision turns on the labor estimate, so that is the number to test before choosing.

Source and limits: GAO's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (GAO-20-195G) describes a life-cycle cost estimate as a structured accounting of all labor, material and other efforts needed to develop, produce, operate and maintain, and dispose of a program, and notes that information technology systems typically incur operating and support costs that are large compared with development and investment: https://gaoinnovations.gov/cost-guide/types-of-cost-estimates.html. All dollar amounts here are invented, and a real comparison would also discount future costs and price risk.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented comparison over four years. Buying means $240,000 of servers with a four-year useful life, no residual value and straight-line depreciation, plus a $12,000 yearly maintenance contract. Renting means a $7,000 monthly ($84,000 yearly) service. Taxes, financing and the time value of money are left out.

Derivation: straight-line depreciation spreads the $240,000 evenly, so the yearly depreciation expense is 240,000 / 4 = $60,000. In year 1, buying uses 240,000 + 12,000 = $252,000 of cash but reports 60,000 + 12,000 = $72,000 of expense; renting uses and reports $84,000.

Independent check over the whole period: four years of depreciation add up to 4 × 60,000 = $240,000, the full purchase cost, so buying reports 4 × 72,000 = $288,000 of expense and also spends 240,000 + 4 × 12,000 = $288,000 of cash. Renting costs 4 × 84,000 = $336,000. The classification moves when the cost is reported, not how much is spent.

Misconception to reject: 'capital spending is free after the first year' or 'operating spending is always cheaper because it starts small.' Capitalized cost returns as depreciation in later years, and a smaller monthly charge can still add up to more over the period.

Change one factor: with a three-year useful life the depreciation becomes 240,000 / 3 = $80,000 a year, so year-1 expense rises to $92,000, above the rental's $84,000, while the four-year cash total stays $288,000.

Source and limits: IAS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment, defines depreciation as the systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount over its useful life, names straight-line as one method and requires day-to-day servicing costs to be recognized in profit or loss as incurred: https://www.ifrs.org/content/dam/ifrs/publications/html-standards/english/2024/issued/ias16.html. US GAAP and tax rules differ in details, and whether a given software or cloud cost can be capitalized is a question for your finance team.

reasoningSteps: Assume payments of 200 now, 55 at year 1 and 60.5 at year 2, plus a hypothetical resale receipt of 121 at year 2. This exercise uses positive costs and negative receipts.
At annual 10%, gross present cost is 200 + 50 + 50 = 300. The present value of the receipt is 100, so net present cost is 200.
